name: Mid-lumbar nerve root (L2, L3 or L4)
description: Irritation or compression of an upper/mid lumbar nerve root as it leaves the spine, typically causing pain or numbness in the front of the thigh, knee or inner shin.

context.text: In a spine-centre study, every patient with L2 or L3 impingement had front-of-thigh pain; L4 impingement more often caused outer-thigh and front-of-shin pain.

In a retrospective neurosurgery series of 1,545 patients with L3/L4 root pain, the prone leg-lift sign (Léri's sign: lying face down, knee bent, leg lifted) reproduced the pain in 93%. Among 153 patients with similar pain but no root compression on imaging, it was negative in about 80%.

name: Low lumbar nerve root (L5 or S1)
description: Irritation or compression of the L5 or S1 nerve root — the classic cause of 'sciatica' running down the back or side of the leg below the knee. The tests that separate L5 from S1 are clinician examinations, so this tool reports them together.

context.text: A Cochrane review found most single physical tests perform poorly at detecting disc-related radiculopathy when used alone.
Pain location can't tell L5 from S1: clinicians shown patients' pain drawings identified the correct root only about 54% of the time, no better than chance.
In primary care, the history alone predicted nerve root compression on MRI about as well as history plus examination (area under the curve 0.80 vs 0.83).

mechanism.text: Compression of the L5 or S1 nerve root, most often by a herniated lumbar disc pressing on the root.

logic.reason: Bending forward raises the pressure in the disc and pulls on the lower roots (the same stretch as the straight-leg raise), so a root pressed by a disc is often worse with it.

name: Lumbar spinal stenosis (narrowed spinal canal affecting several roots)
description: Narrowing of the spinal canal that squeezes several nerve roots at once, typically causing leg pain, heaviness or numbness on walking or standing that eases with sitting or bending forward. Most common in older adults.

mechanism.text: Narrowing of the spinal canal that squeezes several nerve roots at once (the cauda equina), typically worse when standing or walking upright.

name: Sciatic nerve entrapment in the buttock (deep gluteal syndrome)
description: The sciatic nerve is trapped or irritated in the buttock (for example by the piriformis muscle) rather than at the spine. Often called 'piriformis syndrome'.

criteria.title: Michel clinical score for piriformis syndrome (12 points; 8 or more = probable). You can check 6 points here, plus the Beatty self-test in the questions; the other 5 need a clinician.

items.prompt: Do you have buttock pain (one or both sides) that comes and goes, with pain-free periods during the day?

context.text: Across published case reports, the most common features were buttock pain (50–95% depending on how cases are counted), pain made worse by sitting (39–97%), tenderness over the sciatic notch and pain on piriformis-stretching tests. No study has compared these features against people whose sciatica comes from the spine.
Estimates of how common piriformis syndrome is relative to disc herniation vary widely by setting and definition: under 1%, 6% and about 15% in different series.

The Beatty test was designed to be done by the patient. Where it hurts matters: in the original report, 100 people with disc herniation often felt back and leg pain but not deep buttock pain, and 27 people with hip problems felt pain over the outer hip bone instead.

Expert reviewers note that pain on sitting is usually associated with sciatic entrapment beneath the piriformis, while pain on walking just outside the sitting bone suggests ischiofemoral impingement. No study has yet measured how well sitting pain separates these from spinal sciatica.

mechanism.text: The sciatic nerve is trapped in the buttock outside the spine, most often beneath the piriformis muscle (68% of cases in one large series), less often at the sciatic foramen or ischial tunnel.

logic.reason: Coughing or straining raises pressure inside the spine; a nerve trapped outside the spine isn't affected by it.

name: Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
description: A sensory nerve supplying the skin of the lower buttock, back of the thigh and back of the knee. Irritation causes pain or tingling there, often brought on by sitting.

context.text: Neuropathy of this nerve causes pain and tingling over the lower buttock, back of the thigh and back of the knee; sitting pain is a recognised presentation.
Nerve conduction testing of this nerve is difficult, so diagnosis is mainly clinical; in a small series, all 6 suspected cases were confirmed by an ultrasound-guided nerve block.

In two surgical series (17 and 52 patients), every patient had pain on sitting, felt in the buttock, back of the thigh or around the sitting bone; many spent much of the day standing or lying down to avoid it. Most were women.
Half of the patients in the larger series had MRI evidence of a previous hamstring injury.
Its perineal (inferior cluneal) branches can cause sitting pain that overlaps with pudendal neuralgia; targeted nerve blocks are used to tell them apart.

name: Ischiofemoral impingement

name: Cervical nerve root (C5 to C8)

criteria.title: Doha agreement definition of adductor-related groin pain (both required)

items.prompt: Adductor tenderness that you recognise as your pain
Pain in the adductors on resisted adduction (squeezing the legs together)

context.text: The international Doha agreement defines adductor-related groin pain by tenderness of the adductors plus pain on resisted adduction, felt in the adductors rather than elsewhere in the groin.

name: Acromioclavicular (AC) joint pain
description: A joint, not a nerve: pain from the small joint at the top of the shoulder where the collarbone meets the shoulder blade, often worse reaching across the body.

context.text: Tenderness over the AC joint was found in 96% of people with AC joint pain, but the sensitive tests were not specific, so tenderness alone doesn't prove it.

logic.reason: AC joint pain is usually felt exactly over the bony bump where the collarbone ends.
A tendon, joint or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness or pins and needles; those point to a nerve.

name: Shoulder arthritis (glenohumeral osteoarthritis)
description: A joint, not a nerve: wear of the main ball-and-socket shoulder joint, usually in older adults, causing deep aching pain and stiffness.

logic.reason: A worn joint loses movement in several directions, even when someone else moves the arm.
A tendon, joint or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness or pins and needles; those point to a nerve.

name: Neck joint or muscle pain (without a trapped nerve)
description: The neck's joints and muscles, not a nerve root: neck pain that can spread to the shoulder blade and top of the shoulder, without arm numbness or weakness.

logic.reason: Pain from the neck's joints and muscles is usually felt in the neck and changes with head movement.
A tendon, joint or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness or pins and needles; those point to a nerve.

name: Little-finger-side wrist cartilage injury (TFCC)
description: Cartilage and ligaments, not a nerve: injury to the triangular fibrocartilage complex on the little-finger side of the wrist, often after a fall or twisting, causing pain on turning the forearm and gripping.

context.text: In a surgical series the fovea sign was 95% sensitive and 87% specific for ligament tears at this spot; in an unselected clinic study it was much less specific.

logic.reason: A tendon, joint or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness or pins and needles; those point to a nerve.

name: Intersection syndrome (forearm tendon sheath)
description: A tendon problem, not a nerve: painful, often swollen and creaking tendons on the back of the forearm a few finger-widths above the wrist on the thumb side, where the thumb muscles cross the wrist-extensor tendons. Typical after repetitive wrist work, rowing or lifting.

mechanism.text: A narrowed, inflamed sheath around the tendons that pull the wrist back on the thumb side (stenosing tenosynovitis), found at surgery.

context.text: Described as a common painful condition that is infrequently diagnosed.

logic.reason: The condition presents with pain and swelling where the thumb muscles cross the wrist-extensor tendons, a few finger-widths above the wrist.
A tendon, joint or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness or pins and needles; those point to a nerve.
The affected sheath surrounds the tendons that lift the wrist on the thumb side, so loading them should hurt.
Its pain is above the wrist, not at the elbow.

name: Non-specific work-related arm pain (no specific cause found)
description: Forearm, wrist or hand pain linked to repetitive work, such as keyboard, mouse or assembly work, where no specific tendon, joint or nerve problem fits. 'RSI' (repetitive strain injury) is an umbrella term: it also covers specific conditions caused by repetitive use, such as intersection syndrome, De Quervain's, tennis elbow and carpal tunnel syndrome, which are listed as their own options. This option is for repetitive-use pain when none of those fits.

context.text: Work-related upper limb disorders make up 45% of occupational diseases; non-specific arm pain is diagnosed by the absence of specific clinical findings.
People with non-specific arm pain show widespread sensitivity to pressure and temperature without the numbness found in a trapped neck nerve root.
Diagnostic criteria for most soft-tissue arm disorders rely on clinical opinion and have not been shown to be repeatable, sensitive or specific.

logic.reason: By definition the pain is linked to repetitive hand or arm use, and usually eases with rest.

name: Chest wall pain (muscles, ribs or rib cartilage, including costochondritis)
description: Pain that comes from the muscles, bones, cartilage or joints of the chest wall rather than from the heart, lungs or gut. It is usually well localised, often tender when pressed and changed by moving the upper body. It can occur alongside heart disease, so a doctor still needs to rule that out.

mechanism.text: Common causes are inflamed rib cartilage (costochondritis), strained chest muscles, injury to the chest wall, and arthritis of the joints of the breastbone, ribs and thoracic spine; pain can also be referred from the neck.

context.text: Among 1,212 people aged 35 or over who saw their family doctor with chest pain, 565 (46.6%) had chest wall pain. Most often it was behind the breastbone (52.0%) and/or on the left (69.2%), the same places as heart pain.
In Swiss family practices, 300 of 672 people with chest pain (44.6%) had chest wall pain, and in 19 of them it coexisted with coronary heart disease.
Pain brought on by pressing is the most important sign of chest wall pain, but it is not proof: it also happens with other causes.

logic.reason: A joint, bone or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness, pins and needles or burning skin; those point to a nerve.

name: Thoracic nerve root (a nerve leaving the middle of the spine)
description: A nerve root leaving the middle (thoracic) part of the spine is pressed or irritated, for example by a disc bulge, arthritis or diabetes. Each root supplies a strip of skin that wraps from the spine round the side to the front, so pain or altered feeling tends to follow all or part of that strip on one side.

mechanism.text: A thoracic disc herniation can cause pain along the nerve root (radicular pain) and, if it presses on the spinal cord, problems with leg strength and control (myelopathy).

context.text: In 55 people with 72 thoracic disc herniations, 15 (27%) eventually needed surgery; most carried on their daily activities without nerve damage.
When diabetes damages the nerves of the trunk, the pattern varies: sometimes a full band, but in almost two-thirds of episodes only the back or front part of it.

logic.reason: Each thoracic nerve root supplies a strip of skin running from the spine round to the front, so its pain usually follows all or part of that strip on one side.

name: Intercostal nerve (the nerve under a rib), after surgery or injury
description: The nerve that runs along the underside of a rib is damaged or trapped, most often after chest, lung or breast surgery, a chest drain or a rib fracture. Pain, burning or numbness follows the line of that rib, often around a scar.

context.text: Of 488 people interviewed 6 to 30 months after chest surgery, 28.6% still had pain (post-thoracotomy pain syndrome), and in 63% of them it was nerve pain.

logic.reason: This nerve is usually damaged by an operation through the chest wall or an injury to the ribs; without such a history it is a less likely cause.
The nerve runs along one rib, so its pain follows that rib's line.

name: Shingles (herpes zoster) or nerve pain after shingles
description: The chickenpox virus, dormant in a nerve root, reactivates and inflames the nerve. Pain, burning or itching on one side is followed within days by a blistering rash in a strip of skin. Pain can last for months after the rash heals (postherpetic neuralgia). See a doctor promptly if you have a rash: antiviral treatment needs to start early.

mechanism.text: The virus reactivates in a sensory nerve root ganglion and spreads along the nerve to the skin, causing a painful rash in that nerve's strip of skin.
mechanism.locator: Pathophysiology (VZV reactivation in the dorsal root ganglia)

context.text: About 75% of people with shingles have warning symptoms such as pain a few days before the rash appears.
Antiviral treatment should start within 72 hours of the rash appearing.
In 72 people with shingles or its after-effects, the chest and upper-back (thoracic) strips were affected most often (59.7%).
Rarely, the virus causes nerve pain with no rash at all (zoster sine herpete), which makes it hard to recognise.

logic.reason: Shingles is characterised by a painful rash in the affected strip of skin (the pain can start a few days before the rash).
The virus affects one nerve root's strip of skin on one side, so the pain follows that strip.
logic.locator: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis (unilateral, affected dermatome)

name: Notalgia paresthetica (itchy or burning patch beside the shoulder blade)
description: Small skin branches of the nerves of the upper and middle back (T2 to T6) are irritated, giving a long-lasting itch, often with burning, tingling or numbness, in a patch on one side next to or below the shoulder blade. Scratching can darken the skin there.

mechanism.text: Damage to the back skin branches of the T2–T6 spinal nerves, thought to come from pressure by worn spinal joints or by the back muscles the branches pass through.

context.text: Symptoms usually last for years, with periods of remission and flare-ups.

logic.reason: The condition is mainly an itch in a patch of skin, usually on one side, beside or below the shoulder blade.

name: Slipping rib syndrome (loose lower rib tip)
description: The cartilage tip of one of the lower ribs (8th to 10th) moves too much and slips or clicks under the rib above, pinching the nerve that runs beneath it. It gives intermittent, often sharp pain at the lower edge of the ribs or the upper belly, set off by certain movements.

mechanism.text: Too much movement of the front ends of the 8th to 10th ribs lets a rib tip slip under the rib above and press on the intercostal nerve running beneath it.

context.text: In 54 athletes with slipping rib syndrome, symptoms were on one side in 90.7%, and diagnosis took 15.4 months on average.

logic.reason: The loose rib tip slips or clicks under the rib above.

name: Thoracic spine joint or muscle pain (upper or middle back, without a trapped nerve)
description: Pain from the small joints of the thoracic spine, the joints where the ribs meet the spine, or the back muscles. Usually a deep, dull ache close to the spine that changes with posture and movement.

context.text: When the rib-to-spine joints of healthy volunteers were injected to provoke pain, it was a deep, dull ache felt over the joint itself, with no chest wall or arm pain.
Thoracic spine pain is common: 15% to 27.5% of people report some over a year.
context.locator: Abstract, Results (any thoracic spine pain, 1-year prevalence)

logic.reason: Joint and muscle pain usually changes with posture and movement.
A joint, bone or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness, pins and needles or burning skin; those point to a nerve.

name: Spinal compression fracture (often from thin bones, osteoporosis)
description: A vertebra in the spine partly collapses, often with little or no injury in someone with thin bones (osteoporosis). Typical is a sudden, severe back pain that limits ordinary activity. An X-ray shows it, so see a doctor if this seems possible.

context.text: Many compression fractures happen without a clear injury, which makes them hard to recognise.
Women with osteoporosis and a fracture had more severe back pain than those without (6.1 vs 4.3 out of 10).

logic.reason: A joint, bone or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness, pins and needles or burning skin; those point to a nerve.

name: Sternoclavicular joint pain (where the collarbone meets the breastbone)
description: Pain from the joint between the inner end of the collarbone and the top of the breastbone, most often from wear-and-tear arthritis. The joint is tender, may look prominent, and hurts when the shoulders are pushed forward.

context.text: In 44 people with confirmed sternoclavicular joint pain, the joint was tender in 93% and pushing the shoulders forward hurt in 86%; 33 had wear-and-tear arthritis.

logic.reason: Most people with this joint problem feel pain at the joint when they push their shoulders forward.
A joint, bone or muscle problem causes pain, not numbness, pins and needles or burning skin; those point to a nerve.

name: Morton's neuroma (interdigital nerve in the forefoot)
description: An irritated, thickened nerve in the gap between two of the long foot bones, usually behind the 2nd-3rd or 3rd-4th toes. It causes pain in the ball of the foot that can spread into the toes.

context.text: Clinical diagnosis is difficult: reported accuracy ranges from 58% to 93%. Ultrasound, MRI or the response to an anaesthetic or steroid injection are used to confirm it or to exclude other problems.

The probabilities here rest on one small prospective study (Dando: 30 people with forefoot pain, 7 with a neuroma on ultrasound). Only 1 of the review's 9 studies was at low risk of bias, and most included few or no people without a neuroma.

Pinching the gap between thumb and index finger brought on the pain in 95-100% of people with a neuroma in three studies (68% in a fourth, retrospective one), so a painless pinch argues against a neuroma.

logic.reason: 91-92% of people with a neuroma reported pain worse on walking and 81-89% reported relief with rest (three studies, no comparison group).
logic.locator: Table 3, 'Pain aggravated by walking' and 'Rest' rows

logic.reason: Taking shoes off eased the pain in 57-71% of people with a neuroma (two studies, no comparison group).

name: Small toe joint overload (plantar plate tear or toe joint synovitis)
description: A joint problem, not a nerve: strain or tearing of the strong ligament under one of the small toe joints, most often the 2nd, with a sore, swollen joint at the ball of the foot. The toe may slowly drift or lift.

context.text: Plantar plate tears cause forefoot pain and deformity but are often missed on first examination. In one surgical series, 95% had gradual forefoot pain, swelling and a positive drawer test.

logic.reason: 93% of people with a plantar plate tear at surgery had pain that came on gradually.
98% had pain at the 2nd metatarsal head (the ball of the foot under the 2nd toe joint).
95.8% had swelling at the 2nd metatarsal head.
A toe crossing over its neighbour was uncommon in joints without a tear (specificity 88.9%); its absence says little.
A joint, ligament or bone problem without a trapped nerve causes pain, not numbness or pins and needles; those point to a nerve.

name: Metatarsal stress fracture
description: A bone problem, not a nerve: a small crack in one of the long bones of the forefoot from repeated loading.

logic.reason: A stress fracture develops when repeated loading outpaces the bone's repair, so it usually follows a recent rise in activity or a change of shoes or surface.
The pain comes from the bone itself, so one spot on the shaft of a metatarsal is usually sharply tender.
A joint, ligament or bone problem without a trapped nerve causes pain, not numbness or pins and needles; those point to a nerve.

name: Big toe joint arthritis (hallux rigidus)
description: A joint problem, not a nerve: wear of the joint at the base of the big toe, often with a bony bump on top and pain when the toe bends.

context.text: Nerve-like symptoms are common with big toe joint arthritis. Of 98 people, 24.5% reported burning, 14.3% tingling, 12.2% numbness and 56.1% pressure sensitivity (moderate or more), and 30.6% scored as possible or likely neuropathic pain.

logic.reason: All 98 people with painful big toe joint arthritis were tender when the joint was pressed.
97 of 98 had a bony lump that could be felt on top of the joint.
74 of 98 (75.5%) had pain when the joint was moved.
logic.locator: Table 1, 'Pain on motion of first MTP joint'

name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome (tibial nerve at the inner ankle)
description: The tibial nerve or its branches to the sole are squeezed in the tunnel behind the bony bump on the inside of the ankle, causing burning, tingling or numbness in the sole and toes.

logic.reason: The nerve carries feeling from the sole, so pressure on it usually brings numbness or pins and needles there.
Its branches supply most of the sole and the toes, so symptoms usually spread across the sole rather than staying in one gap between two toes.
